summary: Stone 1858 light on northern Lake Champlain: keepers 1859-1931, dark until 2002, now a private residence closed to visitors.

structures.note: 40 ft (12.2 m) from base to centre of lantern per USLHS; LighthouseFriends gives 44 ft (13.4 m).

structures.type: attached to the tower by a passageway
structures.material: granite per USLHS and Rowlett; rubblestone per LighthouseFriends

structures.note: Light moved here in 1931; removed by a Coast Guard contractor on 15 November 2013. LighthouseFriends gives 66 ft tall; Rowlett gives approximately 60 ft (18 m) square.

access.note: Private residence. USLHS lists it as privately owned and not open to the public. LighthouseFriends says the grounds, dwelling and tower are closed.

events.note: The radeau Thunderer sank off Windmill Point while carrying wounded British soldiers from the defeat at Saratoga (LighthouseFriends).
Private light established at the point (LighthouseFriends).
Congress provided $8,000 for a lighthouse at Windmill Point on 3 August 1854.
Octagonal tower built by the contractors Ellis and O'Neil of Malone and Champlain, New York.
Sixth-order Fresnel lens, fixed white, focal plane 52 ft.
Activated with the opening of navigation in 1859 (LighthouseFriends).
Summer kitchen built, old barn removed, new barn and line fence put up; various repairs.
Survey of the reservation and various minor repairs.
In the 1903 season the government lighthouse boat Nettle built a fence at Windmill Point and repaired the buildings.
Light moved from the stone tower to an acetylene light on a steel skeletal tower brought from Crown Point, New York; a lamplighter was hired.
Light left the stone tower; Rowlett marks the stone tower inactive 1931-2002.
Property, minus a half-acre around the steel tower, transferred to the U.S. Customs Service for use against rum-runners during Prohibition.
Light returned to the stone tower on 7 August 2002, National Lighthouse Day; the first relighting on Lake Champlain (LighthouseFriends).
A Coast Guard contractor removed the 66 ft iron skeletal tower on 15 November 2013.
On 16 October 2018 the Coast Guard installed an LED beacon in the lantern room.

corrections.why: 1830 was a private light on the point. The Lighthouse Service's stone tower was built in 1858 and first lit with the opening of navigation in 1859 (LighthouseFriends). USLHS gives 1830 only as the establishment year.

USLHS gives the light's height above mean high water as 52 ft, and Rowlett gives a focal plane of 52 ft (16 m) for the reactivated light; LighthouseFriends gives 52 ft for the 1858 light. The source of the record's 24.4 m is not known; the current Light List entry was not read here, so an editor should check it before applying this.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The 1830 date is a private light that stood on the point before the stone tower. The stone tower was built in 1858 and lit with the opening of navigation in 1859. The 2002 date is the relighting, not a first lighting.
1931 is when the light left the stone tower for the steel skeletal tower. 2002 is when the light returned to the stone tower and the steel tower's light went out (Rowlett gives both).
LighthouseFriends gives a 44-ft tower; USLHS gives 40 ft from base to the centre of the lantern. The record's 12.2 m matches the USLHS figure.

LighthouseFriends describes the 1858 sixth-order lens as a fixed white light; Rowlett gives a white flash every 4 s for the light after its 2002 reactivation. The record uses Rowlett's current characteristic.
USLHS and Rowlett say granite; LighthouseFriends says rubblestone. The story states the disagreement.

notes_for_editor: Not read: the USCG Historian's page on Windmill Point (archived copies were not captured or were refused); the current Light List entry (the source of the record's 24.4 m focal height is not known); the books LighthouseFriends cites (Clifford 1999, Glenn 1994, D'Entremont 2002). Wikipedia was used for leads only: its infobox gives construction 1830, a 40 ft tower and first lit 1858, none cited. The 1949 and 1963 private owners are not named, under the private-residents rule; LighthouseFriends names them. The 1900 Herald and News item about a Mr. Bowman, keeper of the lighthouse, was removed from the story: the report does not name the station, the fisherman was carried toward Windmill Point from the Rouses Point breakwater, and a link to John D. Bowman would rest on name alone. The Bowman roster line rests on the USLHS archive. The 1861 item's word renewed reads from OCR rewivuJ and should be checked on the page image. Rowlett gives a white flash every 4 s for the reactivated light, while LighthouseFriends describes the 1858 lens as a fixed white light; both are recorded. The 1891 and 1893 Light-House Board entries are cited by scan page because the printed page is unconfirmed. The newspaper quotations are OCR text, and the 1903 and 1919 items are OCR-damaged, so their passages are paraphrased. The name of the customs officer in the 1911 item is garbled in the OCR and is not used. LighthouseFriends' claims that Clarinda Mott was the only female keeper in Vermont and was fifty-five on appointment are not confirmed by a second source. A search snippet from New England Lighthouses (not read in full) calls Edward Hill 'Edward H. Hill' and calls him the last keeper, which conflicts with USLHS and LighthouseFriends (Leonard C. Fuller last). Rowlett gives the skeletal tower as about 60 ft square, against LighthouseFriends' 66 ft. The record's staffing is 'unknown'; this file records automation in 1931 from LighthouseFriends. Belair's end of service is not given. The 2002 relighting is documented only by LighthouseFriends and Rowlett.
